character: Plain modern English — the sense of the original, made to read with ease today.
overview: The Lectio Edition renders Aristotle's Ethics in plain modern English that keeps the rigor of the argument while dropping the textbook stiffness — happiness, virtue as a habit, the mean, friendship, and the contemplative life, made to read.
introduction: The Nicomachean Ethics is lecture notes, not a finished book, and it reads like it — compressed, technical, doubling back. That density is the friction most readers hit. The Lectio Edition keeps Aristotle's actual argument intact, every distinction and qualification, but renders it in clear modern English a thoughtful reader can follow without a commentary at hand. The older translations and the Greek stay one tap away.

divergences.note: Older translations render eudaimonia as 'happiness,' and we keep that word because it is what readers expect and what Aristotle's contemporaries called the goal of life. But eudaimonia is not a feeling or mood; it is a whole life that has gone well — literally 'having a good guiding spirit.' Some modern translators prefer 'flourishing' to block the emotional reading. We keep 'happiness' but let Aristotle's own argument redefine it: a complete life of activity in accordance with excellence, not a passing state of pleasure.

Chase and the older tradition say 'virtue,' which now carries a narrow moral or even prudish ring. Areté is broader: the excellence that makes anything good at what it characteristically does — a good knife cuts well, a good harpist plays well, a good person lives well. We render it 'excellence' where the general sense is in play, and keep 'virtue' only where Aristotle clearly means moral character, so the function argument reads as Aristotle meant it: the human good is the soul's activity performed with excellence.

The ergon argument is the spine of Book I. Ergon means a thing's 'work' — what it is for, the activity that is distinctively its own. Older translations say 'work' or 'function'; 'work' can sound like a job, and 'function' can sound mechanical. We use 'function' but gloss it as the characteristic activity that belongs to a human being as such — the use of reason — so the reader sees that Aristotle is asking what a human life is for, not what tasks it performs.

Aristotle builds his whole opening on a pun the English usually loses: ēthikē (the virtue of character) is a slight inflection of ethos (habit). Chase says 'the Greek term denoting it is but a slight deflection from the term denoting custom,' which states the fact but buries the point. We keep 'excellence of character' for the virtue and 'habit' for ethos, and say plainly that the name itself reflects the source — because the etymology IS the argument: character-virtue is not inborn, it is the residue of what we repeatedly do. (We reserve 'virtue' for moral character and 'excellence' for areté in its general sense, as in Book I.)

Mesotēs is the book's signature term: a middle lying between an excess and a deficiency. The older translations vary between 'mean,' 'mean state,' and 'middle state.' We use 'the mean' as the standing term and 'middle' where the spatial image helps, and we preserve Aristotle's crucial distinction between the mean of the thing (the arithmetical midpoint, the same for everyone) and the mean relative to us (what is neither too much nor too little for this person, in this situation) — the distinction that keeps the doctrine from collapsing into 'always pick the middle amount.'

Aristotle rules out two rival accounts of what virtue is — it is not a pathos (feeling) nor a dynamis (capacity) — and concludes it is a hexis: a stable, settled condition of the soul that issues in choice. Chase renders it 'state'; some translators use 'habit,' which blurs it with ethos. We say 'settled state' (and 'disposition' where it reads better) to capture that a hexis is something firm and unshakable, formed by habituation but not identical to habit — the difference between merely doing a just act and being the kind of person from whom just acts reliably flow.

divergences.lectio: voluntary / involuntary (with "up to us" for the related to eph' hēmin)
divergences.note: Chase and the tradition render the pair 'voluntary' and 'involuntary,' and we keep those terms because they are precise and Aristotle's whole analysis of praise, blame, and responsibility is built on them. But hekousion is broader than the legalistic English 'voluntary': it means done willingly, of one's own accord, with the source of the action inside the agent. Where Aristotle presses the underlying idea — that the source 'rests with himself,' to eph' hēmin — we render it plainly as what is 'up to us' or 'in our own power,' so the reader feels the moral stake (we are responsible for our characters) rather than parsing a courtroom word.

Chase says 'Moral Choice'; Ross says 'choice'; others 'purpose' or 'deliberate choice.' The word is the hinge of Book III — for Aristotle it reveals character better than action does. We render it simply 'choice,' adding 'deliberate' where the contrast with mere wanting must be felt, because prohairesis is precisely the wanting that has been reasoned through. Aristotle himself unpacks the etymology — pro- ('before') + hairesis ('a taking/choosing') — as 'what is taken before,' chosen ahead of the alternatives; we keep that play visible where he makes it, since it carries his definition: the voluntary that has first passed through deliberation.

divergences.older: Perfected Self-Mastery / absence of self-control (Chase); temperance / self-indulgence
divergences.note: Chase's 'Perfected Self-Mastery' is accurate but stiff, and his 'destitute of self-control' wrongly suggests akrasia (the weak-willed man who knows better), which is a different vice Aristotle treats in Book VII. We use 'temperance' for sōphrosynē, glossing it once as self-mastery, and 'self-indulgence' for akolasia — the settled, unrepentant pursuit of bodily pleasure, not a failure of will. We also keep Aristotle's pun in III.12: akolasia literally means 'un-chastened-ness' (a- + the root of kolazein, to chastise), which lets him liken the unruly appetite to an unchastened child, so we render the word's roots in the text where he leans on them.

divergences.lectio: greatness of soul; the great-souled person
divergences.note: Chase renders the term "Great-mindedness" and its possessor "the Great-minded man." But the Greek is built from megas (great) and psyche (soul), not from a word for mind, and the modern scholarly tradition (Rackham, Ross, Crisp) has settled on "greatness of soul" and "the great-souled man." We keep that literal compound because the soul, not the intellect, is what Aristotle is sizing up: this is the person who thinks himself worthy of great things and is — worthy because he possesses every excellence, of which greatness of soul is the crown. We render the man as "the great-souled person" rather than "man" for a modern reader, while preserving the portrait's deliberate loftiness. The opposing vices we render "little-souled" (Chase: "Small-minded") and "vain," tracking the same soul-sizing metaphor.

Chase and the older tradition say "Liberality." In current English "liberal" carries political and other senses that pull a reader away from Aristotle's point, which is purely about money — giving and taking it in the right amounts, to the right people, for the sake of what is fine. The Greek eleutheriotes is the excellence of the free person (eleutheros), the one not enslaved to wealth. We render it "generosity," the plain modern word for the giving Aristotle puts at the center of the virtue, and keep "free" in view in the surrounding argument so the reader still feels the original sense: the generous person is the one money does not own.

Aristotle pauses on the etymology of asotia: the asotos is literally the "unsaved" man, the one ruining (wasting) himself by destroying his own substance. Chase keeps the older English "Prodigality," which preserves dignity but obscures the pun on self-destruction. We render it "wastefulness" so the modern reader hears the plain sense Aristotle is unpacking — burning through what you live on — and so the deficiency, aneleutheria (literally "un-freeness," the opposite of generosity), reads naturally as "stinginess," the everyday word for caring too much about money and too little about giving.

segments.text: Every craft and every line of inquiry, and likewise every action and deliberate choice, seems to aim at some good. That is why people have rightly described the good as "what everything aims at." But the aims clearly differ. In some cases the aim is the activity itself; in others it is some product over and above the activity. And where there are products beyond the activities, the products are by their nature better than the activities. Since there are many actions, crafts, and sciences, there are also many aims: health is the aim of medicine, a ship of shipbuilding, victory of generalship, wealth of household management.

Wherever a number of such pursuits fall under a single master art — as bridle-making and all the other trades that produce a horse's equipment fall under horsemanship, and horsemanship together with every military action falls under generalship, and so on — in every case the aim of the master art is more worth choosing than the aims of the arts beneath it, since those lower aims are pursued for the sake of the higher. And it makes no difference whether the activities themselves are the aims, or something further beyond them, as in the sciences just mentioned.

Now if there is some aim of everything we do that we want for its own sake, while we want everything else for the sake of it — and if we do not choose absolutely everything for the sake of something further (for then the chain would run on without end, and our desiring would be empty and pointless) — then plainly this aim will be the good, in fact the highest good. Surely, then, knowing it carries real weight for the conduct of our lives: like archers with a target to aim at, we are more likely to hit what is right. If that is so, we should try to grasp, at least in outline, what this good is and which of the sciences or capacities it belongs to.

One would naturally say it belongs to the most authoritative and most comprehensive of them — and that is plainly the science of the community, the art of statecraft. For statecraft lays down which sciences should exist in a community, which ones each class of citizen should learn, and to what level. We see the most esteemed capacities falling under it — generalship, household management, rhetoric. And since statecraft makes use of all the other practical sciences, and further legislates what people must do and refrain from doing, its aim must take in the aims of the rest, so that this aim will be the human good. For even if the good is the same for an individual and for a community, the good of a community is plainly a greater and more complete thing to attain and preserve. To secure it for one person is something; to secure it for a whole people and for communities is finer and more godlike.

Such, then, is what this inquiry aims at; it is a kind of political inquiry. And we will have treated the subject well enough if we make it as clear as its material allows. Precision is not to be looked for in all discussions alike, any more than in all the products of a craft. What is noble and what is just — the things statecraft examines — vary and waver so much that they are sometimes thought to exist only by convention and not by nature. And even the things agreed to be good show a similar wavering, since harm has come to many people through them: some have been destroyed by their wealth, others by their courage. So we must be content, in speaking about such things and from such starting points, to indicate the truth roughly and in outline. Since we are speaking about what holds for the most part and arguing from premises of the same kind, our conclusions will be of the same sort. Each claim should be received in the same spirit. It is the mark of an educated person to look for exactness in each subject only so far as the nature of the thing allows — it is just as foolish to accept merely probable reasoning from a mathematician as to demand strict proofs from an orator.

Each person judges well the things he knows, and is a good judge of those. So a person educated in a particular subject is a good judge in that subject, and the person broadly educated is a good judge generally. This is why a young person is not a fit student of statecraft. He has no experience of the actions of life, and the whole discussion proceeds from such experience and is about it. And because he tends to follow his feelings, he will listen pointlessly and without benefit, since the goal here is not knowledge but action. It makes no difference whether he is young in years or merely young in character; the defect does not come from age but from living by feeling and chasing each thing as it comes. For such people, like those who lack self-control, knowledge brings no benefit; but for those who shape their desires and act according to reason, knowing these things is of great value. Let this serve as a preface — on the student, on how our remarks should be received, and on what we have set out to do.

Let us pick up the thread. Since all knowledge and every choice reaches for some good, what is the good we say statecraft aims at — the highest of all the goods achievable by action? As far as the name goes, almost everyone agrees: ordinary people and refined people alike call it happiness, and they take living well and doing well to be the same as being happy. But when it comes to what happiness actually is, they disagree, and ordinary people do not give the same account as the wise. Some say it is one of the plain, obvious things — pleasure, or wealth, or honor — and different people say different things; often the same person says different things at different times, calling it health when he is sick and wealth when he is poor. And aware of their own ignorance, people admire anyone who talks grandly over their heads. Others have held that beyond all these many goods there is some single good, existing in itself, which is the cause of all the rest being good.

To sift through every opinion would probably be a waste of effort; it is enough to examine the ones most widely held, or that seem to have something to them. We should not overlook the difference between arguing from first principles and arguing toward them. Plato, too, was rightly puzzled by this, and asked whether the right road runs from first principles or toward them — like the question, on a racecourse, of whether you run from the judges to the far post or back. We must start from what is known. But "known" means two things: known to us, and known without qualification. For us, presumably, we must start from what is known to us. This is why anyone who is going to study what is noble and just, and statecraft generally, with any real profit, must first have been brought up well in good habits. The starting point is the fact that something is so, and if that is clear enough, there is no further need to know why it is so. A person raised this way either already has the right starting points or can take them in easily. As for the person who has neither and cannot acquire them, let him hear Hesiod's verdict: "Best of all is the man who works everything out for himself; good too is the one who takes a good suggestion to heart; but the man who neither thinks for himself nor listens and learns from another — that man is useless."

To return from the digression. People seem, reasonably enough, to form their picture of the good and of happiness from the kinds of lives they lead. The many, the more vulgar sort, take it to be pleasure, and so are content with a life of enjoyment. There are three lives that stand out: this life of pleasure, the life of public engagement, and, third, the life of contemplation. Now the many plainly show themselves to be slavish in choosing a life fit for cattle; yet they get some hearing, because many people in power share the tastes of Sardanapalus. The cultivated and active sort take the good to be honor, which is more or less the aim of public life. But honor seems too shallow to be what we are looking for. It seems to depend more on those who give it than on the person who receives it, whereas we sense that the good must be something of our own, not easily taken away. Besides, people seem to pursue honor in order to convince themselves that they are good: they want to be honored by people of sense, by those who know them, and on the grounds of their virtue. Clearly, then, in their own eyes virtue ranks higher than honor.

So one might suppose virtue is more the aim of public life. Yet even virtue turns out to be not final enough. It seems possible to possess virtue while asleep, or inactive throughout one's life, or — worse — while suffering the greatest misfortunes; and no one would call a person living like that happy, except to defend a thesis. Enough on these lives; they have been discussed sufficiently elsewhere. The life of contemplation we will examine later. As for the moneymaker's life, it is a life under compulsion, and wealth is plainly not the good we are seeking, since it is merely useful, a means to something else. One would sooner take the aims mentioned before to be the good, since at least people value them for their own sake — though they too fall short. Much has been said about them; let us leave them.

We had better also examine the notion of a single universal good, and ask what it could mean, even though the inquiry is awkward because the people who introduced this theory of Forms are friends of ours. Still, it is surely better — indeed a duty, where the truth is at stake — to give up even our own views, especially since we are lovers of wisdom. Both our friends and the truth are dear to us, but it is right to honor the truth first. Now those who put forward this theory did not posit Forms for classes where they spoke of before and after, which is why they did not make a Form of numbers. But good is spoken of in the category of substance, in quality, and in relation; and what exists in itself — substance — is by nature prior to what is relative, which is a kind of offshoot of being. So on their own principles there could be no single common Form covering all these.

Furthermore, good is spoken of in as many ways as being itself: in the category of substance (God, or intelligence), in quality (the virtues), in quantity (the right amount), in relation (the useful), in time (the right moment), in place (a habitation), and so on. So good plainly cannot be some single common thing, universal and one; otherwise it would not have been spoken of in every category but in one only. And third: since the things falling under a single Form are studied by a single science, there would be just one science of all goods together — whereas in fact there are many sciences even of the goods in a single category. The right moment, for instance, is studied in war by generalship, in illness by medicine; the right amount, in food by medicine, in exercise by athletics. One might also ask what on earth they mean by "the thing itself," since the account of humanity is one and the same in "man himself" and in any particular man. Insofar as both are man, they do not differ at all; and if so, then "good itself" and any particular good will not differ insofar as both are good. Nor is good made any more good by lasting forever, since something white for a long time is no whiter than something white for a day.

The Pythagoreans seem to give a more convincing account when they place "the One" in their column of goods, in their double list of goods and bads — and Speusippus seems to have followed them in this. But these matters belong to another occasion. There is an obvious objection to what I have said: the theory was not meant to apply to all goods, but only those pursued and valued for their own sake belong under one Form, while whatever tends to produce or preserve these, or to prevent their opposites, is called good only because of them, in a derivative sense. Clearly, then, things are called good in two ways: some in themselves, others for the sake of these. So let us separate the goods that are good in themselves from the merely useful ones, and ask whether the former are spoken of under a single Form. But which goods should we count as good in themselves? Should it be all those pursued even in isolation — like understanding, sight, certain pleasures and honors, which we do pursue with some further end in view but would still count among the goods worth having in themselves? Or is nothing good in itself except the Form, in which case the Form would amount to nothing?

If, on the other hand, these things are goods in themselves, then the account of what makes them good should be the same in all of them, as the account of whiteness is the same in snow and in white lead. But it is not: the accounts of what makes honor, understanding, and pleasure good are distinct and different. So the good is not some common thing answering to a single Form. Then how does the one name come to be shared, since it does not look like mere coincidence? Are different things called good because they all derive from one source, or all contribute to one end — or rather by analogy, so that as sight is to the body, intelligence is to the soul, and so on? But perhaps we should drop these questions for now; pursuing them precisely belongs to another branch of philosophy. The same goes for the Form. Even if there is some single good predicated in common of all good things, or some good existing separately and on its own, it plainly could not be acted on or attained by a human being — and what we are looking for is exactly that. Someone might think it would still help to know the universal good as a model, so as to know better which goods are within our reach and, knowing them, to attain them. The argument has some plausibility, but it is contradicted by how the crafts actually work. Every craft aims at some good and seeks to supply what is missing, yet they get along without any knowledge of the good itself. It is hardly likely that all craftsmen alike should be ignorant of so great an aid and not even look for it. And it is hard to see how a weaver or a carpenter would be helped in his own work by knowing this good itself, or how someone would be a better healer or general for having gazed on the Form. The doctor does not even study health in this abstract way, but the health of human beings — or rather of this or that patient, since he treats individuals. So much for these matters.

Let us return to the good we are seeking. What can it be? It plainly differs from one action and craft to another: it is one thing in medicine, another in generalship, and so on. What is the good in each? Surely it is that for the sake of which everything else is done — health in medicine, victory in generalship, a house in building, and in each case something else; in every action and choice it is the end, since for the sake of this people do everything else. So if there is some single end of everything we do, this will be the good attainable by action; and if there are several, then these will be. The argument, after circling back, has reached the same point as before, and we must try to make it still clearer. The ends are evidently many, and some of them — wealth, flutes, instruments generally — we choose for the sake of something else; so plainly not all ends are final. But the highest good is clearly something final. So if there is only one final end, that is what we are seeking; and if there are several, the most final of them.

We call an end that is pursued for its own sake more final than one pursued for the sake of something else; and we call an end never chosen for the sake of anything else more final than ends that are chosen both in themselves and for the sake of that further end. So what is always chosen for itself and never for the sake of anything else is final without qualification. Happiness above all seems to be of this kind, since we always choose it for itself and never for the sake of anything else. Honor, pleasure, intelligence, and every excellence we do choose for themselves — we would choose each even if nothing came of it — but we also choose them for the sake of happiness, supposing that through them we will be happy. No one, though, chooses happiness for the sake of these, or for the sake of anything else at all.

The same conclusion follows from the notion of self-sufficiency, which is thought to belong to the final good. By self-sufficient we do not mean sufficient for a person living a solitary life, but for his parents and children and wife as well, and in general his friends and fellow citizens — since a human being is by nature made for a community. Some limit must be set here, of course, for if we extend it to parents and descendants and friends of friends it will go on without end; but this we can leave for later. For now we take the self-sufficient to be that which, all by itself, makes life worth choosing and lacking in nothing. And such, we hold, is happiness. Moreover, we take happiness to be the most choiceworthy of all things — and not as one good counted alongside others. For if it were so counted, then adding even the smallest further good would plainly make it more choiceworthy than before; the addition would be that much more good, and of two goods the greater is always more choiceworthy. So happiness is plainly something final and self-sufficient, the end of everything we do.

But to call happiness the highest good is perhaps to say something everyone accepts, and what we still want is a clearer account of what it actually is. We can get this by grasping the work, the characteristic function, of a human being. For a flute player, a sculptor, any craftsman — anyone, in general, who has a function and an activity — the good and the doing-well are thought to lie in that function. The same should hold for a human being, if there is a function that belongs to a human being as such. Are we to say that a carpenter and a cobbler have their functions and activities, but a human being as such has none and is left by nature with no work to do? Surely, just as the eye, the hand, the foot, and each part has its own function, we should suppose a human being too has some function beyond all of these. What could it be? Not merely being alive — that is shared even with plants, and we are looking for what is peculiar to us. So we set aside the life of nutrition and growth. Next would come the life of perception, but this too is shared, with horses and oxen and every animal. What remains is a life of action belonging to the part of us that has reason. Of this, one part has reason in the sense of obeying it, the other in the sense of having it and exercising thought. And since "the life of reason" itself can mean either the capacity or its actual exercise, we should take it as the active exercise, since that is more properly called living.

If, then, the function of a human being is an activity of the soul in accordance with reason, or not without reason; and if we say that the function of a given thing and of a good one of that kind are the same in type — a harpist and a good harpist, and so on across the board, adding to the function its excellence (the harpist's function is to play the harp, the good harpist's to play it well) — if all this holds, then we take the human good to be the function performed well: an activity of the soul in accordance with excellence, and if there are several excellences, in accordance with the best and most complete. And we must add: in a complete life. For one swallow does not make a spring, nor does one fine day; and in the same way one day, or a short time, does not make a person blessed and happy. Let this stand as a rough sketch of the good. Probably the right way is to draw the outline first and fill it in afterward, and anyone could carry forward and complete what has been well sketched; time is a good discoverer and collaborator in such things. That is how the arts have advanced — anyone can supply what is missing.

Remember, too, what was said before: do not demand the same exactness in everything, but in each thing the kind that suits its subject and is proper to the inquiry. A carpenter and a geometer ask about the straight line in different ways: the carpenter only so far as it serves his work, the geometer asking what it is and what its properties are, since he is after the truth. We should proceed the same way in other matters, so that side issues do not overgrow the main ones. And do not demand the reason why in everything alike; in some cases it is enough that the fact has been well established, as with first principles, where the fact comes first and is itself the starting point. Some first principles are grasped by induction, some by perception, some by a kind of habituation, others in other ways. We should try to approach each according to its nature and take pains to define them well, since they carry great weight for what follows. The starting point seems to be more than half the whole, and many of the things we are seeking come to light once it is clear.

We should examine happiness not only from our conclusion and the premises of our argument, but also in light of what people commonly say about it — for with the truth all the facts harmonize, while the false soon clashes with how things really are. Goods are commonly divided into three kinds: external goods, goods of the soul, and goods of the body, and we call the goods of the soul good in the fullest and truest sense. Now we take the actions and activities of the soul to be where happiness lies, and these belong to the soul. So our account agrees with this opinion, which is an old one and accepted by philosophers. We are also right to say that the end consists in certain actions and activities, since this puts it among the goods of the soul and not the external ones. Our account fits the common view that the happy person lives well and does well, since we have made happiness more or less a kind of living well and doing well.

All the things people look for in happiness seem to be present in our account. Some think happiness is virtue, some practical wisdom, some a kind of theoretical wisdom; some think it is these together with pleasure, or at least not without pleasure; others throw in external prosperity as well. Some of these views are held by many people or are very old, others by a few but distinguished men, and it is unlikely that either group is wholly wrong; more likely each is right on at least one point, or on most. Our account agrees with those who say happiness is virtue, or some virtue, since activity in accordance with virtue belongs to virtue. But there is an important difference between locating the good in a possession and locating it in a use — between a settled state and an activity. A state can be present in someone without producing any good — in a person asleep, say, or otherwise inactive — but an activity cannot, for it will necessarily act, and act well. And just as at the Olympic games it is not the finest and strongest men who are crowned but those who actually compete (the winners come from among them), so in life it is those who act rightly who carry off the noble and good things.

Their life is also pleasant in itself. Feeling pleasure is something internal to the soul, and each person finds pleasant the things he is said to love: a horse to the horse lover, a show to the lover of shows, and in the same way just acts to the lover of justice, and in general the things that accord with virtue to the lover of virtue. For most people the things they find pleasant conflict, because they are not pleasant by nature; but to those who love what is noble, the things pleasant by nature are pleasant — and actions in accordance with virtue are such, so that they are pleasant both to such people and in themselves. So the good person's life has no need of pleasure as some added ornament; it contains its pleasure within itself. For, besides what was just said, a person who takes no pleasure in noble actions is not even good — no one would call a person just who takes no pleasure in acting justly, or generous who takes none in generous acts, and so on. If that is right, then actions in accordance with virtue must be pleasant in themselves. They are also good and noble, and supremely so, if the good person judges rightly about them — and he judges as we have said.

So happiness is the best, the noblest, and the most pleasant thing, and these are not separated as in the inscription at Delos: "Justice is noblest, health is best, but to get what you long for is sweetest." For all three belong together in the best activities, and we say that happiness is these activities, or the one that is best. Still, happiness plainly also needs external goods, as we said. It is impossible, or at least not easy, to do noble actions without resources: many things are done by means of friends, wealth, and political power, as if by instruments. And the lack of some things spoils our blessedness — good birth, fine children, good looks. A person who is repulsive in appearance, or low-born, or solitary and childless is not really capable of happiness, and still less, perhaps, one whose children or friends are thoroughly bad, or who has lost good ones to death. So, as we said, happiness seems to need this kind of prosperity as well; which is why some identify it with good fortune, while others identify it with virtue.

This raises a question: is happiness something that can be learned, or acquired by habit or some other training, or does it come by some divine allotment, or even by chance? Now if the gods give anything to human beings, it is reasonable that happiness is a gift of theirs, especially since it is the best of human things. But this may belong to another inquiry. Even so, it is clear that even if happiness is not sent directly by the gods but comes through virtue and some kind of learning or training, it is still among the most godlike things; for the prize and end of virtue is plainly the best thing there is, something divine and blessed. On this view it would also be widely shared, since it could belong, through learning and effort, to anyone not crippled for virtue. And if it is better to be happy this way than by chance, that itself is a reason to think it is so, since whatever is by nature is naturally as fine as it can be — and likewise whatever is by art or by any cause, above all the best cause. To leave the greatest and noblest thing to chance would strike a badly false note. The answer is also clear from our definition: happiness is an activity of the soul in accordance with a certain kind of excellence. Of the other goods, some must be present as preconditions, and others are by nature useful as instruments.

This agrees with what we said at the start: we took the end of statecraft to be the best thing, and statecraft devotes its greatest care to making the citizens people of a certain kind — good, and apt to do what is noble. With good reason, then, we do not call an ox or a horse or any other animal happy, since none of them can take part in such activity. For the same reason a child is not happy either: because of his age he cannot yet do such things, and when we call a child happy we are predicting on the basis of his promise. For happiness requires, as we said, complete virtue and a complete life. Many reversals and all kinds of chances occur over a lifetime, and the most prosperous person may fall into great misfortunes in old age, as the heroic poems tell of Priam; and no one calls a person happy who has met such a fate and died in misery.

Are we then to call no one happy while he lives, and, as Solon advised, look to the end? And if we hold to that, is a person actually happy once he is dead? Or is that completely absurd, especially for us, who say happiness is a kind of activity? But suppose we do not call the dead person happy, and Solon did not mean that either, but only that one can safely pronounce a person happy once he is finally beyond evils and misfortunes — even this is open to dispute. For it is thought that something good or bad can reach a person who is dead, just as it can reach someone alive who is unaware of it: honor and dishonor, and the good or bad fortune of his children and descendants generally. This raises a further difficulty: a person may live in blessedness to old age and die accordingly, and yet many changes may come about through his descendants — some of them may flourish and get the life they deserve, others the reverse, and clearly they may stand in all sorts of relations to their ancestor. It would be strange for the dead person to shift along with them and become now happy, now wretched; but it would also be strange if the fortunes of descendants made no difference at all, for no time, to their ancestors.

But we should return to the earlier question, since its answer will settle the present one. If we are to look to the end and only then call a person blessed — not as being so but as having been so earlier — surely it is absurd that, at the very time when he is happy, the truth of it cannot be asserted, just because we are unwilling to call the living happy on account of their exposure to change, and because we have conceived of happiness as something stable and not easily altered, whereas fortune keeps revolving around the same people. For clearly, if we follow people's fortunes, we will often call the same person happy and a little later wretched, presenting our happy person as a kind of chameleon, built on no firm ground. Surely this is not right — to track our verdict to the swings of fortune. For our doing well or badly does not rest in fortune; human life merely needs it as an accessory, as we granted, while it is the activities in accordance with virtue that decide our happiness, and their opposites that decide the reverse.

And the question we just discussed bears witness to our account. For nothing in human affairs has the stability of the activities in accordance with virtue; they are thought to be more lasting even than the sciences, and the most valued of them are the most lasting, because the blessed live in them most fully and most continuously — which seems to be why such activities are not forgotten. So the happy person will have the stability we are after, and will keep it throughout his life. He will always, or above all, be doing and contemplating the things that accord with virtue, and he will bear the chances of life most nobly and gracefully in every way, being truly good and "foursquare without reproach." Many things happen by chance, differing in size; the small strokes of good or bad fortune plainly do not tip the balance of a life, but the great and repeated ones, if they go well, will make life more blessed, since by their nature they add grace and the use of them is noble and good; and if they go badly, they crush and maim our blessedness, bringing pain and obstructing many activities. Yet even here nobility shines through, when a person bears many great misfortunes with good grace — not from any dullness to pain, but because he is noble and great-souled.

And if the activities are what govern a life, as we said, then no one among the blessed can become wretched, since he will never do what is hateful and base. The truly good and sensible person, we believe, bears all his fortunes becomingly and always does the noblest thing the circumstances allow — just as a good general makes the best use of the army he has, and a good cobbler makes the finest shoe from the leather given him, and so with every other craftsman. If that is right, the happy person can never become wretched — though he will not be blessed, of course, if he meets a fate like Priam's. Nor is he unsteady and easily turned. He will not be dislodged from his happiness lightly, nor by ordinary misfortunes, but only by great and repeated ones; and after such blows he will not recover his happiness in a short time, but, if at all, over a long and complete stretch in which he has won great and noble things. Why, then, should we not call happy the person who is active in accordance with complete virtue and is adequately furnished with external goods — not for some passing period, but over a complete life? Or should we add that he must also go on living so and die accordingly, since the future is hidden from us, and we take happiness to be in every way an end and complete? If so, we will call those among the living blessed who have and will have the things we have described — blessed, but as human beings are blessed.

Let this much settle these points. Now to hold that the fortunes of descendants and of friends in general contribute nothing at all to the condition of the dead seems too cold a view, and against what people commonly believe. But since the things that happen are many and differ in all sorts of ways, some touching us nearly and others lightly, to go into every distinction would be a long and endless task; it is enough to speak in outline. As with a person's own misfortunes — some have weight and turn the balance of a life, others are lighter — so it is with those that befall his friends. And it makes a great difference whether those affected are alive or dead, far more than whether the crimes and horrors in a tragedy are merely assumed in the background or actually carried out before us. We should take this difference into account, and still more, perhaps, the open question whether the dead really share in any good or evil at all. From all this it seems that if anything does reach them, good or bad, it must be something faint and small, either in itself or to them — at any rate not great or strong enough to make happy those who are not, or to take away the blessedness of those who are. So the good or bad fortunes of friends do touch the dead somewhat, but not in such a kind or degree as to turn the happy unhappy, or to do anything like that.

With these points settled, let us examine whether happiness belongs among the things we praise or among the things we honor as precious — for it plainly is not a mere capacity. Whatever we praise, we praise for being of a certain kind and standing in a certain relation to something else. We praise the just person, the brave person, the good person generally, and virtue itself, because of their actions and results; and we praise the strong man and the fast runner for being of a certain nature and standing in a certain relation to something good and fine. This is clear from the praise of the gods, which comes out ridiculous when they are measured against our standard — and that happens because all praise, as we said, involves reference to a standard. But if praise is for such things, then what applies to the best things is not praise but something higher and better. And so it is: we call the gods blessed and happy, and we call those people blessed who come nearest the gods. The same holds for goods: no one praises happiness the way he praises justice; he calls it blessed, as something more godlike and better.

Eudoxus, too, seems to have argued well for pleasure's claim to the highest prize. The fact that pleasure, though one of the goods, is not praised he took as a sign that it is superior to the things that are praised — a superiority he assigned also to a god and to the good, since these are the standard to which everything else is referred. For praise belongs to virtue, since virtue makes us apt to do noble things, while celebration in words belongs to definite achievements of body or mind. But pursuing this precisely belongs more to a treatise on praise; for us it is enough that what has been said shows happiness to belong among the things that are precious and final. And it seems to be so also because it is a starting point: it is for the sake of happiness that we all do everything else, and we take the source and cause of good things to be something precious and divine.

Since happiness is an activity of the soul in accordance with complete excellence, we should examine excellence; for that will probably give us a clearer view of happiness as well. The true statesman, moreover, is thought to have taken the most pains over this, since he wants to make the citizens good and obedient to the laws — the lawgivers of the Cretans and the Spartans are examples, and any others like them. If this inquiry belongs to statecraft, then clearly pursuing it is in keeping with our original plan. The excellence we are to examine is, of course, human excellence, since the good and the happiness we were seeking were a human being's. And by human excellence we mean not that of the body but that of the soul, since we say happiness is an activity of the soul. If so, the statesman plainly must know something about the soul, just as the eye doctor must know about the body as a whole — and all the more, since statecraft is more precious and higher than medicine; indeed the better doctors take great pains over knowledge of the body. So the statesman too must study the soul, but with his own ends in view and only so far as his inquiry requires; to carry the study to greater precision is more laborious than his purpose demands.

A few things have been said about the soul well enough in popular discussions, and we may use them here: that the soul has two parts, one without reason and one having reason. (Whether these are actually separate, like the parts of the body and everything divisible, or are two only in account while being by nature inseparable, like the convex and concave of a curve, makes no difference for our purpose.) Of the part without reason, one element seems shared with all living things and is vegetative — the cause of nutrition and growth; one would assign such a power of the soul to everything that takes nourishment, even to embryos, and the same power to full-grown creatures, which is more likely than that it should be a different one. The excellence of this part is plainly not peculiar to human beings but shared; for this part and this power are thought to be most active in sleep, when the good person and the bad are least distinguishable — whence the saying that for half their lives the happy are no different from the wretched. And reasonably so, since sleep is an inactivity of the soul in the respect in which it is called good or bad — except that to some small degree some of its movements get through, so that the dreams of decent people are better than those of ordinary ones. But enough of this; we may set the nutritive part aside, since by its nature it has no share in human excellence.

There seems to be another part of the soul without reason, which nonetheless shares in reason in a way. In the self-controlled person and in the one who fails at self-control alike, we praise the reasoning part of the soul, the part that has reason, because it urges them rightly toward the best. But there is plainly in them, alongside reason, something else by nature, which fights and strains against reason. Just as paralyzed limbs, when a person means to move them right, swerve off to the left, so it is with the soul: the impulses of people who lack self-control run counter to reason. The difference is that in the body we see the part that swerves, while in the soul we do not. Still, we should suppose there is in the soul too something besides reason, opposing it and running against it — how it is distinct does not matter here. This part, too, plainly shares in reason, as we said: in the self-controlled person it obeys reason, and in the person of real temperance and in the brave person it is still more obedient, since in them it speaks entirely with the same voice as reason.

So the part without reason is itself twofold. The vegetative part has no share in reason at all; but the appetitive part, desire in general, shares in it in a way, insofar as it listens to reason and can submit to its rule. This is the sense in which we say a person "listens to reason" from a father or friends — not the sense in which we speak of the reason, the account, of a mathematical truth. That the part without reason is in some way won over by reason is shown by correction and by every kind of rebuke and encouragement. And if we are to say this part too has reason, then the part that has reason will itself be twofold: one part has reason strictly and in itself, the other has it in the way a child heeds its father. Excellence, too, is divided along this line. We call some excellences intellectual and others of character: theoretical wisdom, understanding, and practical wisdom are intellectual; generosity and temperance are excellences of character. When we speak of a person's character we do not call him wise or quick-witted, but even-tempered or temperate; yet we do praise the wise person too, for his state of mind — and the praiseworthy states are the ones we call excellences.

Excellence comes in two kinds: excellence of intellect and excellence of character. The intellectual kind owes both its origin and its growth mostly to teaching, which is why it needs experience and time. Excellence of character, by contrast, comes from habit — and that is reflected even in its name, since the Greek word for it is only a slight inflection of the word for habit.

This makes one thing clear at once: none of the virtues of character arises in us by nature. Nothing that exists by nature can be trained into a different way by habit. A stone, which by nature falls downward, could never be trained to rise, not if you threw it up ten thousand times to accustom it; fire cannot be habituated to burn downward; and in general nothing that behaves one way by nature can be made by habit to behave another. So the virtues come about in us neither by nature nor against nature. Rather, nature gives us the capacity to receive them, and habit brings that capacity to completion.

Consider further: in everything we have by nature, we are equipped with the capacity first and put it to use afterward. The senses make this plain. We did not acquire sight or hearing by seeing or hearing repeatedly; the reverse is true — we had the senses and then used them, we did not get them by using them. But the virtues we acquire by first putting them into practice, exactly as we acquire any skill. The things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them: people become builders by building and harpists by playing the harp. In the same way, we become just by doing just acts, self-controlled by doing acts of self-control, and brave by doing brave acts.

What happens in communities bears this out. Lawgivers make the citizens good by habituating them, and this is the aim of every lawgiver; those who fail to do it well miss their mark — and it is just here that a good constitution differs from a bad one.

Moreover, every virtue is both produced and destroyed by the very same kind of acts — and so is every skill. It is by playing the harp that both good and bad harpists are made, and likewise builders and all the rest: build well and you become a good builder, build badly and you become a bad one. If this were not so, there would be no need for teachers at all; everyone would have been born already good or bad at his craft. It is the same with the virtues. By how we conduct ourselves in our dealings with others, some of us become just and others unjust; by how we conduct ourselves in the face of danger, growing accustomed to fear or to confidence, some become brave and others cowards. The same goes for situations involving appetite and anger: some people become self-controlled and even-tempered, others uncontrolled and hot-tempered, depending on how they behave in such situations. In a word, our settled states are produced by acts of the same kind as themselves. That is why we must give our acts a certain quality, since our states take their character from the differences in our acts. So it makes no small difference whether we are habituated one way or another straight from childhood — it makes a very great difference, or rather it makes all the difference.

Now the point of the present inquiry is not, as it is in some others, mere knowledge. We are not investigating what virtue is just in order to know it, but in order to become good — otherwise the inquiry would be useless. So we have to look at how to perform our actions, since, as we have said, our actions decide what sort of states we form. That we should act in accordance with right reason is common ground, and we will take it for granted here; later we will say what right reason is and how it stands to the other virtues.

But let one thing be agreed between us from the start: any account of how to act can only be given in outline, not with precision. As we said at the very beginning, the kind of treatment demanded must suit the subject, and matters of action and of what is good for us have nothing fixed about them, any more than matters of health do. And if the general account is as inexact as this, the account of particular cases is even less precise, for such cases fall under no craft and no set of rules. The agents themselves must, in each instance, look to what the occasion demands — just as happens in medicine and in navigation. Still, even though our subject is like this, we must try to offer what help we can.

First, then, notice this: states like these are by their nature destroyed by deficiency and by excess. We can see it in the cases of strength and health (since for things we cannot observe we have to use evidence we can): too much exercise ruins strength, and so does too little; likewise too much food and drink, or too little, ruins health, while the right amount produces it, increases it, and preserves it. It is the same with self-control and courage and the other virtues. The man who runs from everything and fears everything and stands his ground against nothing becomes a coward; the man who fears nothing at all and marches against everything becomes reckless. In the same way, the man who indulges in every pleasure and abstains from none becomes dissipated, while the man who shuns all pleasure, like a boor, becomes a kind of insensible blank. So self-control and courage are destroyed by excess and by deficiency, and preserved by the mean.

And there is more. Not only are these states produced, increased, and ruined by the same kinds of acts; their exercise, once they are formed, takes place in the same kinds of acts as well. This holds for more observable things too, like strength: strength comes from eating plenty and working hard, and the strong man is the one best able to do just that. It is the same with the virtues. By abstaining from pleasures we become self-controlled, and once we are self-controlled we are best able to abstain from them. And so with courage: by training ourselves to make light of frightening things and to stand up to them we become brave, and once brave we are best able to stand up to them.

We should treat the pleasure or pain that follows on our acts as a sign of the state we have formed. The man who abstains from bodily pleasures and is glad to do so is self-controlled; the man who abstains but resents it is not. The man who stands up to danger and either enjoys it or at least feels no pain is brave; the man who does it in distress is not. For excellence of character is concerned with pleasures and pains: it is because of pleasure that we do what is base, and because of pain that we shrink from what is fine. This is why, as Plato says, we should have been trained from childhood to feel pleasure and pain at the right things; this is what right education means.

There is further evidence. Since the virtues have to do with actions and feelings, and every action and feeling is attended by pleasure or pain, here too virtue turns out to be concerned with pleasure and pain. The fact that we use punishments to correct people points the same way, for punishments are a kind of cure, and cures by their nature work through opposites. Recall, too, what we said before: every state of the soul has its nature and exercises itself in relation to the very things that naturally make it better or worse — and it is through pleasures and pains that states become bad, namely by pursuing or avoiding the wrong ones, or at the wrong times, or in the wrong way, and so on. This is why some people actually define the virtues as a kind of freedom from feeling, a state of calm. But they are wrong to put it without qualification, instead of adding "in the right way" and "in the wrong way," "at the right time," and the rest. We may take it, then, that virtue is the kind of state, with respect to pleasures and pains, that does what is best, and that vice is the opposite.

The following will make the same point clear. There are three things that move us to choose and three that move us to avoid: the fine, the advantageous, and the pleasant, and their three opposites — the shameful, the harmful, and the painful. About all of these the good man tends to go right and the bad man to go wrong, but most of all about pleasure. For pleasure is something we share with all animals, and it is bound up with everything we choose, since both the fine and the advantageous strike us as pleasant. What is more, the feeling for pleasure has grown up with us all since infancy, which makes it hard to scrape away, dyed as it is into our very lives. And, to a greater or lesser degree, we even use pleasure and pain as the measure of our actions. For all these reasons, our whole business has to be with pleasure and pain, since getting our pleasures and pains right or wrong matters enormously for how we act. As Heraclitus says, it is harder to fight pleasure than to fight anger — and skill and virtue alike always concern themselves with what is harder, since in what is hard, doing well counts for more. So this is one more reason why virtue, and the study of conduct generally, must devote itself entirely to pleasures and pains: handle these well and you will be good; handle them badly and you will be bad.

Let us take it, then, as established that virtue is concerned with pleasures and pains; that it is increased or ruined by the same kinds of acts that bring it into being, used in the right or the wrong way; and that it exercises itself in the same kinds of acts out of which it arose.

Now someone might be puzzled by our claim that to become just we must do just acts, and to become self-controlled we must do acts of self-control. "For," he would say, "if people are already doing just and self-controlled acts, then they are already just and self-controlled — just as someone who does what is grammatical or musical is already a grammarian or a musician." But the case is not even like that with skills. A person may do something grammatically correct by chance, or because someone else prompted him; he is a grammarian only when he both produces something grammatical and produces it as a grammarian does — that is, out of grammatical knowledge of his own.

And in any case skills and virtues are not parallel. The products of a skill have their merit in themselves, so it is enough that they turn out a certain way. But acts done in accordance with virtue are not done justly or with self-control merely because they themselves are a certain way; the doer must also be in a certain condition when he does them. First, he must act knowingly; second, he must choose the act, and choose it for its own sake; and third, he must do it from a firm and unshakable character. For having a skill, these conditions do not count — only the knowledge does. For having a virtue, the knowledge counts for little or nothing, while the other conditions count for everything — and it is precisely by doing just and self-controlled acts again and again that we come to meet them. So acts are called just and self-controlled when they are the kind of acts a just or self-controlled person would do; but the person who does them is not yet just or self-controlled unless he also does them as the just and self-controlled do. We are right, then, to say that a person becomes just by doing just acts and self-controlled by doing self-controlled ones; without doing them, no one has even a chance of becoming good. But most people do not do them. They take refuge in talk and suppose that they are doing philosophy and that this will make them good — behaving rather like patients who listen carefully to the doctor and then do nothing he prescribes. Such patients will never be healthy in body; and people who philosophize like that will never be healthy in soul.

Next we must ask what virtue is. The things that arise in the soul are of three kinds — feelings, capacities, and states — so virtue must be one of these. By feelings I mean appetite, anger, fear, confidence, envy, joy, love, hatred, longing, jealousy, pity — in general, whatever is attended by pleasure or pain. By capacities I mean what we have in virtue of which we are able to have these feelings: the capacity, for instance, by which we are able to feel anger or pain or pity. By states I mean what we have in virtue of which we stand well or badly toward these feelings — toward anger, for example, we stand badly if we feel it too violently or too weakly, and well if we feel it in the balanced way; and so on for the rest.

Now the virtues and vices are not feelings, because we are not called good or bad on account of our feelings, but we are on account of our virtues and vices; and because we are neither praised nor blamed for our feelings as such — a man is not praised simply for being afraid or angry, nor blamed simply for being angry, but only for being so in a particular way — whereas we are praised and blamed for our virtues and vices. Again, we feel anger and fear without choosing to, whereas the virtues are a kind of choice, or at any rate involve choice. And besides, we are said to be "moved" by our feelings, but as for the virtues and vices, we are not said to be moved but to be in a certain condition. For these same reasons, the virtues are not capacities either, since we are not called good or bad, nor praised or blamed, simply for being able to have feelings. And we have our capacities by nature, but we do not become good or bad by nature, as we said earlier. So if the virtues are neither feelings nor capacities, the only thing left is that they are states.

That settles what kind of thing virtue is, in its genus. But we must not stop at saying it is a state; we must say what sort of state it is. Here is the point. Any excellence both brings the thing that has it into good condition and makes it perform its work well. The excellence of an eye makes both the eye good and its work good, since it is by the eye's excellence that we see well. The excellence of a horse makes a horse good — good at running, at carrying its rider, at standing up to the enemy. If this holds in every case, then the excellence of a human being will be the state that makes a person good and makes him perform his own work well. We have already said how this comes about, but it will be clearer still if we look at the particular character that virtue has.

In anything continuous and divisible, you can take a larger part, a smaller part, or an equal part — and this either in the thing itself or relative to us; and the equal is a mean between excess and deficiency. By the mean of the thing I mean the point equidistant from each extreme, which is one and the same for everyone. By the mean relative to us I mean the amount that is neither too much nor too little — and this is not one and the same for everyone. Take a quantity: if ten is too much and two too little, then as a matter of arithmetic six is the mean of the thing, since it exceeds two by the same amount that ten exceeds it. But the mean relative to us cannot be found that way. It does not follow that if ten pounds of food is too much to eat and two too little, the trainer will prescribe six; for even six may be too much or too little for the particular person — too little for Milo the wrestler, too much for a beginner. The same goes for how much running or wrestling to do. In this way every expert avoids excess and deficiency and looks for the mean — not the mean of the thing, but the mean relative to us — and chooses that.

If, then, every skill does its work well by keeping its eye on the mean and steering its products toward it — which is why people say of a thing in good condition that you could not add anything to it or take anything away, on the assumption that excess and deficiency destroy what is good while the mean preserves it; and if good craftsmen, as we say, work with their eye on the mean; and if excellence, like nature, is more precise and better than any craft — then excellence too must aim at the mean. I mean excellence of character, since that is what is concerned with feelings and actions, and these admit of excess and deficiency and the mean. It is possible, for instance, to feel fear, confidence, appetite, anger, pity, and pleasure and pain in general too much or too little, and both are wrong. But to feel these things when we ought, at the things we ought, toward the people we ought, for the reasons we ought, and in the way we ought — that is the mean, and the best, and the mark of virtue. In the same way, actions too admit of excess, deficiency, and the mean. Virtue is concerned with feelings and actions, and in these excess is wrong and deficiency is blamed, while the mean is praised and gets it right — and praise and rightness both belong to virtue. So virtue is a kind of mean, in that it aims at what is intermediate.

Consider, besides, that there are many ways to go wrong (since, as the Pythagoreans put it, the bad belongs to the unlimited and the good to the limited), but only one way to go right. That is why going wrong is easy and going right is hard — easy to miss the target, hard to hit it. So for this reason too excess and deficiency belong to vice, and the mean to virtue: "Good in one way only, bad in every way."

Virtue, then, is a settled state that issues in choice, lying in a mean relative to us, a mean defined by reason — the reason by which the person of practical wisdom would define it. It is a mean between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. And it is a mean in this further sense: the vices fall short of, or overshoot, what is right in both feelings and actions, while virtue finds the middle and chooses it. So in respect of its essence and the account that states what it is, virtue is a mean; but in respect of what is best and right, it is an extreme — the peak.

Not every action or feeling, however, admits of a mean. Some have names that already imply badness — spite, shamelessness, envy; and among actions, adultery, theft, murder. These and their like are condemned because they are bad in themselves, not because there is too much or too little of them. With them you can never be right; you are always wrong. Rightness and wrongness in such cases do not depend on doing them to the right person, at the right time, in the right way; simply to do any of them at all is to be wrong. You might as well demand a mean, an excess, and a deficiency in acting unjustly, or in cowardice, or in dissipation — for then there would be a mean of excess and a mean of deficiency, an excess of excess and a deficiency of deficiency. But just as there is no excess or deficiency of self-control or courage, because the mean is in a way the peak, so there is no mean of these bad things, and no excess or deficiency of them either; however they are done, they are wrong. In short, there is no mean of an excess or a deficiency, and no excess or deficiency of a mean.

It is not enough, though, to state this in general; we have to fit it to particular cases. In discussions of conduct, general statements cover more ground but say less that is true, while statements about particulars are truer to life — because action deals with particulars, and our account has to square with those. So let us take our particulars from the following table.

With fear and confidence: the mean is courage. Of those who go too far, the man who exceeds in fearlessness has no name (many of these states do not), and the man who exceeds in confidence is reckless; the man who has too much fear and too little confidence is a coward.

With pleasures and pains — though not all of them, and with fewer pains than pleasures: the mean is self-control, and the excess is dissipation. People deficient in the pursuit of pleasure hardly occur, so this character too has no name; but since such a person is conceivable, let us call him insensible.

With giving and taking money, first on the ordinary scale: the mean is generosity, the excess wastefulness, the deficiency stinginess. Here the two extremes go to excess and deficiency in opposite respects: the wasteful man gives out too much and takes in too little, the stingy man takes in too much and gives out too little. (We are giving only an outline and summary here, on purpose; we will draw these distinctions more exactly later.)

With money on the grand scale: there is a mean called magnificence — the magnificent man differs from the merely generous one, since magnificence deals with large sums and generosity with small. The excess here is called tastelessness or vulgar display, the deficiency pettiness; these too differ from the extremes that go with generosity, and we will say later how they differ.
With honor and dishonor, on the great scale: the mean is greatness of soul, the excess is what we might call vanity, the deficiency smallness of soul.

With honor on the small scale: there is a state related to greatness of soul as generosity is related to magnificence — concerned with small honor rather than great. A man may reach for honor more than he should or less than he should; the one who reaches too far is called ambitious, the one who falls short unambitious, and the one who is just right has no proper name. The states have no names either, except that the disposition of the ambitious man is called ambition. This is why both extremes lay claim to the middle ground as contested territory, and why we ourselves sometimes call the right character ambitious and sometimes unambitious, and praise now the one and now the other. Why we do this will be explained later; for now let us go through the rest of the virtues on the plan we have laid down.

With anger: here too there is excess, deficiency, and a mean. They have no settled names, but since we call the right character even-tempered, let us call the mean even temper. Of the extremes, let the man who goes too far be called hot-tempered and his fault hot temper, and the man who falls short spiritless, and his fault a lack of spirit.

There are also three further means that resemble one another but differ. All three have to do with how we behave in words and deeds when we are with others. They differ in that one is concerned with truth in such things, the other two with what is pleasant — one of these in relaxation and amusement, the other across the whole of social life. We should say a word about these too, so as to see more clearly that in everything the mean is praiseworthy, while the extremes are neither right nor praiseworthy but blameworthy. Most of these also lack proper names, but we will try, as before, to coin some, for clarity's sake.

With truth about oneself: the man in the mean we may call truthful, and his state truthfulness. As for misrepresenting oneself, if it tends toward exaggeration it is boastfulness and the man a boaster; if toward understatement it is irony, or self-deprecation, and the man self-deprecating.
With what is pleasant in relaxation and amusement: the mean is wit, and the man witty; the excess is buffoonery, and the man a buffoon; the man who falls short is a boor, and his state boorishness.

With what is pleasant in the rest of social life: the man who is as he should be is friendly, and his mean friendliness; the man who overdoes it, if from no motive of his own, is obsequious, and if to get something out of it, a flatterer; the man who falls short and is unpleasant in everything is contrary and quarrelsome.

There are means in our feelings and in matters involving feeling as well. Modesty, for instance, is not a virtue, but the modest person is praised. Here too one person is said to be in the mean, another in the excess — like the bashful man who is overcome with shame at everything — while the person who feels no shame at all is shameless; the one in between is modest. And righteous indignation is a mean between envy and spite. All three have to do with the pleasure or pain we feel at what happens to our neighbors: the man with righteous indignation is pained at undeserved good fortune; the envious man overshoots him and is pained at anyone's good fortune; and the spiteful man falls so far short of being pained that he actually rejoices at others' misfortune. But there will be another occasion to discuss these, and justice too, since justice is spoken of in more than one sense; afterward we will treat each precisely and show how they are means. We will do the same for the intellectual excellences.

Since there are three dispositions in each case — two of them faults, one in the way of excess and one in the way of deficiency, and one of them right, the mean — they are all in a way opposed to one another. The extremes are opposed both to the mean and to each other, and the mean is opposed to the extremes. Just as the equal is larger compared to the smaller and smaller compared to the larger, so the mean states are excessive compared to the deficient ones and deficient compared to the excessive ones, in feelings and in actions alike. The brave man looks reckless next to the coward and cowardly next to the reckless man; the self-controlled man looks dissipated next to the insensible man and insensible next to the dissipated; the generous man looks wasteful next to the stingy man and stingy next to the wasteful. So the extreme characters each push the man in the middle toward the other side: the coward calls the brave man reckless, the reckless man calls him a coward, and so on. And because of this mutual opposition, the extremes are more contrary to each other than either is to the mean, since they stand farther from each other than from the middle — just as the larger and the smaller stand farther from each other than either does from the equal.

There is this too: some extremes bear a certain resemblance to the mean — recklessness to courage, wastefulness to generosity — but the extremes are utterly unlike each other. Now things that stand farthest apart are defined as contraries, so the farther apart, the more contrary they are. In some cases it is the deficiency that is more opposed to the mean, in others the excess. Cowardice, the deficiency, is more opposed to courage than recklessness, the excess; but dissipation, the excess, is more opposed to self-control than insensibility, the deficiency. There are two reasons for this. One comes from the nature of the thing itself: when one extreme is nearer and more like the mean, we set not it but the other against the mean as the true opposite. Since recklessness seems nearer and more like courage, and cowardice less like it, we set cowardice rather than recklessness against courage, because what stands farther from the mean seems more contrary to it. The other reason comes from ourselves. The things we are naturally more inclined toward seem more opposed to the mean. We are naturally inclined more toward pleasures, and so we slide more readily into dissipation than into decorum. We call "more contrary," then, the extreme we tend to drift into — which is why dissipation, the excess, is more contrary than insensibility to self-control.

So we have now said enough about how excellence of character is a mean; how it lies between two faults, one of excess and one of deficiency; and how it is such because it aims at the middle in both feelings and actions. This is also why being good is hard work. In each case finding the middle is hard, just as finding the center of a circle is not something anyone can do, but only the one who knows how. Anyone can get angry — that is easy — and anyone can give away money or spend it; but to do these to the right person, in the right amount, at the right time, for the right reason, and in the right way — that is not something anyone can do, and it is not easy. That is why doing it well is rare, and praiseworthy, and fine.

So the man aiming at the mean should first steer clear of the extreme more opposed to it — as Calypso advises in Homer, "Keep the ship clear of this spray and surge." For of the two extremes one is always more of a mistake than the other; and since hitting the mean exactly is so hard, the next-best course, as they say, is to take the least of the evils. We will do this best by the method just described. We should also watch for our own natural bias, which differs from person to person and shows itself in the pleasures and pains we feel. And we should drag ourselves off in the opposite direction, for by pulling well clear of where we go wrong we will arrive at the middle — the way people straighten warped timber. In everything, we should be most on guard against what is pleasant, and against pleasure itself, since we are not impartial judges of it. We ought to feel toward pleasure the way the elders of Troy felt toward Helen, and say of it what they said of her — for if we send it away, we will go wrong less often.

In short, by taking these precautions we will best be able to hit the mean. Still, this is no doubt hard, especially in particular cases. It is not easy to determine exactly how, with whom, for what, and for how long one should be angry; we ourselves sometimes praise people who fall short and call them even-tempered, and at other times call the hot-tempered manly. And the person who deviates a little from what is right, whether toward too much or too little, is not blamed; only the one who deviates a good deal is, since he cannot go unnoticed. But just how far and how much someone has to go to be blameworthy is not easy to fix in words — no easier than anything else that is a matter of perception. Such things lie among the particulars, and the judgment rests with perception. This much, at least, is clear: the mean state is praiseworthy everywhere, but we have to lean sometimes toward excess and sometimes toward deficiency, since that is the easiest way to hit the mean — and so to get it right.

Virtue has to do with how we manage our feelings and our actions, and praise and blame attach to actions that are voluntary, while for the involuntary we make allowances and sometimes even feel pity. So anyone trying to understand virtue has to draw the line between what is voluntary and what is not. The distinction matters for lawmakers too, when they decide whom to honor and whom to punish.

Involuntary actions seem to come in two kinds: those done under compulsion, and those done out of ignorance.
