Such a person must be counted good: someone who loves the truth as such, and is truthful where it makes no difference, will be all the more truthful where it does, since he will shun falsehood as base, having shunned it even for its own sake. And such a person is praiseworthy. Still, he leans rather toward understating than overstating, since that seems to be in better taste — exaggeration being so tiresome. The man who lays claim to more than he has with no further motive looks like a base sort, since otherwise he would take no pleasure in falsehood; but he comes off as a fool rather than a knave. The one who does it with a motive — for honor or glory, like the braggart — is not so very blameworthy; but the one who does it, directly or indirectly, for money is uglier. The braggart is a braggart not by his ability but by his choice, by his settled state and the kind of man he is — just as one liar takes pleasure in falsehood for its own sake while another lies out of a hunger for reputation or gain. Those who exaggerate for reputation claim the sort of qualities that win praise and congratulation; those who do it for gain claim qualities their neighbors can make use of, and whose absence can be hidden — being a skilled seer, say, or a good doctor. So most people pretend in this direction and exaggerate here, since these are the qualities that pay.

The false-modest, who play down their own qualities, come across as the more refined, since they are thought to speak not for gain but to avoid grandstanding. One very common trait in them is to disown the things people generally admire — as Socrates used to do. Those who lay false claim to small things, and to things whose falseness is obvious, are called poseurs and are contemptible. Sometimes this very modesty looks like boasting, as with the studied plainness of dress the Spartans go in for; both excess and the extreme of deficiency have something of boasting in them. But people who practice understatement in moderation, and about things not too plainly false, give an impression of refinement. Here it is the boaster who seems opposed to the truthful person, as the worse character.

Since life has its breaks and in them makes room for amusement with a touch of humor, it seems there is a fitting way to behave here too — a sense of the kind of thing to say and how to say it, and likewise of what to listen to. There is a difference between saying such things and hearing them. Here too there is an excess, a deficiency, and a mean. People who overdo the laughable are thought buffoons and vulgar, grabbing at a laugh any way they can, at any cost, bent on raising one rather than on saying what is seemly and sparing the target of the joke. Those who would never crack a joke themselves and are annoyed by anyone who does are thought boorish and stiff. The ones who joke in good taste are called witty — "nimble," really, since their wit is a kind of nimbleness of character, and just as we judge bodies by their movements, so we judge characters. But because the laughable lies near at hand and most people enjoy fun and joking more than they should, the buffoons too get called witty, as if they were charming. That they differ, and by a good deal, is plain from what has been said. Another thing belonging to the mean is tact: it is the tactful person who says and listens to the things that befit a decent and well-bred man, since there are things it suits such a man to say and hear by way of humor, and the humor of a gentleman differs from that of a vulgarian, as the educated man's does from the boor's. You can see this by comparing the old comedy with the new: in the old, the fun came from obscenity; in the new, more from innuendo — and that is no small difference where decency is concerned. Should we then define the man who jokes well by his saying what befits a gentleman, or by his not paining the target, or even by his giving pleasure? Or is any such definition vague, since different things are hateful and pleasant to different people? Whatever he says, he will also listen to, since a man is thought to do what he can stand to hear — though there is a limit; he will not do quite everything he will listen to, since a joke is a kind of abuse, and lawgivers forbid certain kinds of abuse and perhaps should have forbidden certain jokes too. So the refined and gentlemanly man is, as it were, a law to himself. Such is the person in the mean, whether you call him tactful or witty. The buffoon cannot resist the laughable, sparing neither himself nor anyone else so long as he gets his laugh, saying things no man of refinement would say, and some he would not even put up with hearing. The boor is useless for such company: contributing no fun of his own, he is sour with everyone who does. Yet some rest and amusement in life are generally agreed to be necessary. So the three means we have described all occur in life, and all concern the give-and-take of words and deeds. They differ in that one is concerned with truth, and the other two with what is pleasant: of these two, one deals with the humor of life, the other with the rest of social intercourse.

To call shame an excellence is not right, since it is more like a feeling than a settled state. It is defined as a kind of fear of disgrace, and its effects are much like those of the fear of danger: people who feel shame turn red, and people who fear death turn pale. Both, then, are plainly bodily in some way, which is thought a mark of a feeling rather than a settled state. The feeling, moreover, does not suit every age, only youth. We think the young should be capable of shame, since living by feeling as they do, they go wrong often, and shame holds them back. We praise the young for being modest, but no one would praise an older man for being prone to shame, since we think he ought not to do anything that calls for it. For shame, arising at base actions, does not belong to a good man at all, since such actions should not be done in the first place — and it makes no difference whether some things are disgraceful in truth and others only in opinion, since neither should be done, so that one ought not to be in a position to feel shame at all. To be the kind of man who does something disgraceful is the mark of a bad character. To be the kind who would feel shame if he did, and to count that as being good, is absurd, since shame is felt only at voluntary actions, and a good man will never willingly do anything base. Shame may be good on a condition — "if he were to do such a thing, he would feel shame" — but the excellences are good without conditions, not just in supposed cases. And granting that shamelessness, not blushing to do what is disgraceful, is base, it still does not follow that it is good to do such things and then feel shame. Self-control, likewise, is not properly an excellence but a kind of mixed state — but all that will be set out in a later book.
